docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am a forestry undergraduate at Universitas Riau, currently in my final year. My work so far has moved between the field and the desk: supervising excavation sites for boundary compliance in Riau, measuring forest plots for an above-ground biomass study on peatland, and digitizing land cover data from satellite imagery at RECOFTC. On the analysis side I use QGIS, ArcGIS, Google Earth Engine, and Python (Pandas, Matplotlib).

Alongside those, I built Flood Coverage, an independent analysis of whether a satellite actually observes a flood while it is rising, measured across four river basins in Europe and Indonesia from one year of Sentinel-1 acquisition metadata.

I am looking for entry-level roles in GIS analysis, remote sensing, or environmental data work, preferably connected to forest monitoring.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Selected work in geospatial analysis, forestry, and data science.

BioSift

Web app that checks the quality of GBIF species occurrence records. Ten automated quality checks, spatial outlier detection, and Darwin Core Archive export. Built for the 2026 GBIF Ebbe Nielsen Challenge.

Python Streamlit GBIF scikit-learn folium

View Project

Flood Coverage

Measures how often a Sentinel-1 pass lands inside a flood's rise, across four river basins in Europe and Indonesia, and whether a GloFAS forecast peak can actually be checked. One year of real acquisition metadata, computed locally.

Python STAC Sentinel-1 GloFAS JavaScript

View Project

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BioSift is an open-source web app for checking the quality of species occurrence records from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). GBIF aggregates data from thousands of publishers, and before a dataset is used for analysis it helps to know how reliable it is: whether coordinates are missing or misplaced, whether records are duplicated, and where coverage gaps are. BioSift automates those checks. Enter one or more species names, set a year range, and the app fetches the records from the GBIF API, scores them, and reports the results.

Study area: Global Year: 2026 Role: Solo project Status: Completed; submitted to the 2026 GBIF Ebbe Nielsen Challenge

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data source

  • GBIF.org occurrence records, retrieved through the public API

Processing steps

  1. Fetch occurrence data from the GBIF API with filters for year range, basis of record, and record limit
  2. Run ten automated quality checks: missing coordinates, zero coordinates, duplicate records, coordinate-country mismatch, low coordinate precision, and temporal gap detection
  3. Produce spatial diagnostics: an interactive point map, heatmaps, DBSCAN-based outlier detection, and a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) preview of the species distribution
  4. Score each record for reliability on a 0–100 scale and rate the dataset's fitness for five scientific use cases
  5. Export results as CSV, reliability-scored CSV, or a Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A)

Tools

Tool Purpose Python + Streamlit Web application pygbif GBIF API access pandas Data cleaning and filtering folium + plotly Interactive maps and charts scikit-learn DBSCAN spatial outlier detection scipy Kernel Density Estimation

docs.title: What the App Does
docs.text:
• Runs ten quality checks and summarizes each dataset with a data health score from 0 to 100%
  • Compares up to five species side by side and exports the comparison as a report
  • Generates a methods paragraph and GBIF dataset citations in APA or BibTeX format
  • Exports cleaned records as CSV or Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A)
  • Runs in the browser with no installation; the source code is public

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Flood Coverage asks a question that flood maps do not answer: if a flood rises over the next six hours, will a satellite see it while it is rising?

Public flood mapping has largely solved speed. Copernicus GFM publishes a global 20 m flood layer in under eight hours for more than 99% of scenes, and the fastest documented activation delivered its first extent eight hours after trigger. The limit that remains is not processing time but how rarely the satellite looks, compared with how fast the water moves. A basin can be described as monitored on every dashboard while a short flood passes entirely between two passes.

The project measures that gap from real acquisition metadata rather than assuming it, and then pairs the result with the free GloFAS discharge forecast that already exists for each basin, to ask whether the forecast peak can be verified at all.

Study areas Po river plain (IT), Ahr valley (DE), Siak (Riau, ID), Ciliwung (Jakarta, ID) Period 1 November 2025 to 1 November 2026 Role Solo project Status Working analysis and demo, source public

docs.title: The measurement
docs.text:
The probability is computed empirically, not modelled. Take the real acquisition timestamps for a year, slide a rise window across them in one hour steps, and count how often a look falls inside the window.

P(rise observed) = windows containing at least one look / all windows

Passes cluster, so the answer differs sharply from the nominal revisit figure. The same run also reports the gap distribution, so any rise time can be read off without re-running.

docs.title: Results, one year and one collection
docs.text:
Basin Looks per year Looks per day Median gap 6 h rise seen 48 h rise seen Po, Italy 315 0.87 24.0 h 21% 91% Ahr, Germany 250 0.69 24.0 h 17% 91% Siak, Riau 78 0.22 120.1 h 5% 39% Ciliwung, Jakarta 51 0.14 203.3 h 3% 28%

The Po and the Ahr have almost the same cadence, 0.87 and 0.69 looks per day and a 24 hour median gap, and they land in completely different places: 90% against 17% at a six hour rise. Nothing about the satellites changed between them. The rise time did. Jakarta's median gap of 203 hours means a flash flood is essentially never observed while it is rising, and its longest blackout in the year ran 288 hours, from 22 September to 4 October 2026.

docs.title: Can the forecast be checked?
docs.text:
GloFAS already issues a free 30 day river discharge forecast for every basin here, so prediction is not the hard part. Each forecast peak is paired with the measured chance that a look lands within 24 hours of it.

Basin Forecast peak Date (2026) Versus 30 day median Checkable within a day Po 2746.9 m³/s 22 Nov 3.2x 91% Ahr 5.7 m³/s 15 Nov 6.8x 91% Siak, Riau 447.8 m³/s 23 Nov 3.6x 39% Ciliwung, Jakarta 34.0 m³/s 24 Nov 4.8x 28%

Europe can check its own forecast. Jakarta cannot: for 72% of forecast peaks no look lands within a day, so the forecast is issued, acted on, and never verified.

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data sources

  • Sentinel-1 GRD acquisition metadata, queried through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API
  • GloFAS v4 river discharge forecast, through the Open-Meteo forecast API
  • Esri World Dark Gray basemap, for the locator map only

Processing steps

  1. Search the STAC API for each basin's bounding box over the 12 month window
  2. Deduplicate polarisation pairs so each overpass counts once
  3. Compute the gap distribution, the median and 95th percentile gap, and the count of gaps over 48 hours
  4. Slide the rise window across the record in one hour steps to estimate the observation probability at 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 72 and 168 hours
  5. Pull the GloFAS forecast per basin on a 3x3 sampling grid, keeping the cell with the highest median discharge, because the basin centroid often falls on a headwater cell
  6. Pair each forecast peak with the measured probability that a look falls within 24 hours of it

Tools

Tool Purpose Python standard library Ingest, statistics, and the web server STAC API (HTTP + JSON) Sentinel-1 acquisition metadata Open-Meteo API GloFAS discharge forecast HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript The page, with no build step MapLibre GL JS Locator map of the basin boxes

The analysis runs on the Python standard library alone: no dependencies, no API keys, no build step. Every statistic on the page is computed locally from the downloaded metadata.

docs.title: What the app does
docs.text:
• Shows, per basin, the share of randomly timed floods of a chosen rise length that contain at least one acquisition
  • Draws the whole sweep from 3 to 168 hours, so the conclusion can be read at any rise time instead of resting on one assumption
  • Renders the full year as a strip, one tick per acquisition, with every gap drawn at its true length
  • Reports the longest blackout in the year and how many separate floods would fit inside it
  • Pairs today's GloFAS forecast peak with the measured chance that it can be confirmed by a look

docs.title: What it does not tell you
docs.text:
• No acquisition is not no flood. A gap means no look, not absent water, and nothing is rendered as zero.
  • Rise times are assumptions, not per-event measurements, which is why the page shows the full sweep.
  • GloFAS covers rivers only, on a grid that does not resolve small steep catchments, and it is not a flood warning.
  • Four basins do not describe the world. Both European basins sit inside the acquisition scenario that plans them for frequent revisit, and the Indonesian pair shows how far below that coverage can fall.
  • This is a personal analysis, not a peer reviewed study.
